members.title: 《山河旅探》团队新作：能联机的“盗梦空间”？

news.body:
如果《盗梦空间》成为现实，你会和朋友一起去哪里冒险？
又或者纵身跃入深不见底的旋涡，赌一把下面还有另一层梦境？
这些画面，很容易让人产生一个念头：如果把《盗梦空间》做成联机游戏，大概就是这种感觉。
更令人没想到是，它背后的开发团队，竟然是奥秘游戏！没错，就是曾推出《山河旅探》和《我在地府打麻将》的奥秘！根据团队公布的资料，《山河旅探》累计销量已超过100万套，目前Steam简体中文评测好评率为96%，处于“好评如潮”档位。
这次的新作名叫《潜梦者》，是一款以梦境为主题的多人合作冒险游戏。从清末探案，到地府搓麻，再到组队盗梦，奥秘选择新题材的跨度，每次都会令人瞳孔放大。
从游戏PV来看，游戏整个玩法似乎是“搜躲撤”，用“盗梦空间版致命公司”来理解或许更直观。你和朋友们一起潜入游戏主角梦境，搜集道具，合作解密并躲避怪物，并且在最后一起撤离。当然，还有个很合理的限制：得赶在人家睡醒之前走。
而这游戏吸引人的地方，还在于它真的很适合拿“梦”来做场景。
城市可以上下颠倒，楼房向着不可能的方向堆叠；迷雾里露出巨像的轮廓，雷雨云中又有鲸鱼翻飞。现实里放在一起很难解释的东西，到了梦里，反而有了一种奇怪的说服力。
游戏里也有中式梦核的元素。熟悉的办公室、带着童年记忆气息的场景，被放进了这些不太正常的空间里。这里的微妙之处在于，你认识其中的东西，却不一定认识它们拼出来的地方。
当然，带上朋友之后，梦境冒险也可能随时变成大型互坑现场。
游戏支持2—4人合作，玩家可以举起、抛出队友，组成四人“人链”，也可以配合完成“空中接人”。 这些动作光是想想，就很容易脑补出两种结果：配合得好，大家一起过关；配合不好，下次聚会又多了一个可以反复提起的话题。毕竟，敢让朋友把自己扔出去，多少需要一点信任。
《致命公司》《R.E.P.O.》已经让不少玩家发现，和朋友一起应对危险，本身就能制造很多乐趣。《潜梦者》则在这之外，把梦境的美术表现也当成了一个看点。让人想拉朋友来的，除了合作和互坑，还有那些值得一起进去看看的奇异场景。
这也是近年国产游戏让人期待的地方：从大型动作游戏到各具特色的独立作品，越来越多团队开始尝试不同的类型，多人合作自然也有继续打磨的空间。场景能不能更讲究，关卡能不能更有意思，都值得往下做。
至于《潜梦者》能否把这些想法接起来，还得等实际玩到才能下结论。
不过，至少现在，已经有了个把它发进朋友群的理由：下次联机，去别人梦里开黑？

members.title: 万圣诡夜降临西部荒原，《遥遥西土》节日更新现已上线

news.body:
《遥遥西土》节日更新现已上线。官方表示，乌鸦在雕像上盘旋，南瓜在月光下狂飞，前所未见的鬼影正潜伏在暗处.....又到了一年百鬼夜行的万圣节，牛仔们！是时候点亮火球术了！
仿佛1年365天都在和骷髅精怪搞联欢的，可能是最适合万圣节气息的法国独立游戏《遥遥西土》万圣节限时版本，现已正式上线！同时，《遥遥西土》将同步开启20%OFF限时折扣，到手价57.6元持续两周。同一天，游戏原声OST也将登陆各大主流流媒体平台，在未来也会上架steam，欢迎牛仔们在荒原之外继续听个够。
本次更新，《遥遥西土》不仅带来了万圣节主题活动、全新地图和包括皮肤在内的多项全新系统，还有三个Boss战的全面重做，以及超50项Bug修复，足够爽玩一整个万圣季！
这次更新，从进入游戏那一刻，万圣节的气息就会扑面而来。
你再熟悉不过的酒馆，笼罩在一层诡异氛围中，火车后方不知何时多出了一口冒着幽光的坩埚。
这口坩埚就是本次万圣节活动的核心，而要让它运转起来，你需要深入各个地图去收集祭品。
你会在荒野中遇见栖息着乌鸦的神秘雕像，靠近后这些乌鸦会惊慌逃窜，射落它们即可收集羽毛。
在某些角落里，你还会撞见闹鬼的墓地，成群的骷髅脱离地面疯狂飞旋，将它们逐一击碎就能收获骷髅。
而最珍贵的南瓜资源则只能通过击杀本次活动的全新万圣节Boss获得，这位拥有独特招式的新Boss将是整场活动中最具挑战性的对手。
带着这三种资源回到大厅后，前往火车后方新增的坩埚处即可进行仪式，完成仪式将产出万圣节活动专属货币闹鬼蜡烛，这些专属代笔可以用来兑换三套角色皮肤、一套坐骑马匹皮肤，以及多个称号和幽灵主题表情。
其实，万圣节活动只是本次更新的一部分，在活动之外，多项新内容也会同步上线。
首先是全新的冒险场景红杉地图，张牙舞爪的诡秘林地、不时飞过的漆黑乌鸦、高悬在天空的那轮冷冷的月亮，都在等着给你一场月光光心慌慌的冒险体验。
除此之外，全新的任务也即将到来，来看看这个诡异的西部，这次又将带来什么样的故事？
这个更新还添加了一个新的副手武器——喷气背包。玩家可以一下飞到空中然后重重砸向敌怪，你可曾见过一招从天而降的掌法？
最让人意想不到的是，本次更新竟然还加入了赛马玩法，在紧张刺激的赏金任务之余，牛仔们现在可以跨上坐骑与同伴一较高下，在西部荒原上来一场酣畅淋漓的策马狂奔。
另外还有死灵法师、酒馆和秃鹫这三场Boss战已获得全面重做，三位Boss都获得了全新的攻击模式和行为逻辑，战斗节奏与以往完全不同。
在困难和噩梦难度下，这三位Boss还会触发进化机制，展现出更具威胁性的全新形态和技能组合，为追求顶级挑战的队伍带来真正的考验。
更别提，现在动态难度系统，也就是所谓的干扰/调整项也已经加入游戏。在地图上找到交易NPC激活调整项，给你的冒险增加更多意想不到的“惊喜”。
当然，《遥遥西土》的技术团队，也没有忘记在带来刺激的同时，优化牛仔们的冒险体验，这次，全新的视觉表现已进入西部世界，如果你仔细看，现在破败的木屋、长满苔藓的废弃机器都更加逼真细致了。
在看不到的地方，涵盖战斗、任务、装备和性能等多个方面的超过100个Bug得到了处理，其中包括沼泽戏法在双持左轮手枪上仍会造成自伤的问题、吟游蛮人猛击后可能卡入异常动画的问题、高换弹速度阻止扇击王牌连锁触发的问题都已经消失，你可以好好发挥你的bd之力了！
《遥遥西土》20%折扣正在开启中，折后价57.6元。
万圣之夜，西部难眠！快拿起你的武器（也有可能是乐器），在月光下与同伴一起狩猎吧！

members.title: 用动作肉鸽，写一卷上古时代的洪荒史诗｜《定海》试玩体验

news.body:
大禹失踪，洪水复涨，天柱早已折断，神仙们也各有各的算盘。此时站出来说“我来”的，是一个被剥夺了名字、死了数百年的神将。
他借了大禹义子的身体，身体原主则变成一只圆滚滚的鸟，在旁边对他冷嘲热讽。这一对奇妙的组合该如何进入《山海经》的画卷，又会给玩家带来怎样的体验呢？
《定海》是一部杰仕登自研的单人动作 RPG Roguelike，2.0 试玩版现在已登陆 PC Steam，并参加了10月的新品节。它使用了《山海经》中的古代神话传说，人称与游戏的叙事方式却不同寻常：玩家操控的是夺取“益”之躯体的玄龙，“益”却变成一只会在旅途中插话、吐槽的羽嘉幼雏；一人一鸟穿过不周山、壶岫、河阳，寻找失踪的大禹。
洪荒题材最容易落入一个圈套：名号一个比一个大，玩家做的事却和杂兵无双里的先锋官没区别，变成一种反复殴打七彩小龙虾的体验。而《定海》把“定海”这个宏大的命题，拆成了每局的小事：选兵器、清据点、设法宝、打灵兽、带着材料回神珍铁，再去解决下一片土地的麻烦。
鲧治水用堵，《山海经·海内经》说他“窃帝之息壤以堙洪水”；禹改用疏导，在外十三年，“过家门不敢入”（《史记·夏本纪》）。一局一局的轮回，就是“堵—疏—再堵—再疏”的演练。在这里，玄龙本来就是个死过一次、不肯散场的残魂，死亡不是暂停键，而是世界观的一部分。你不需要接受“主角为什么能无限复活”，因为游戏一上来就告诉你：这具身体是抢来的，这条命是捡来的。
更妙的一层，是《山海经》本来就是一本“分类学”的书。它不给你完整故事，只一段一段列山、列水、列异兽。
刘歆说“益等类物善恶，著《山海经》”，益就是那个给万物分类的人。游戏让益当主角，等于让记录者走进自己的记录；每局抽法宝、灵兽、词条，本质上就是一本可执行的《山海经》目录。
在此之上是玩法：动作与挑战。神话的尺度得用身体去量。相柳九首、刑天断首，玩家站三十米外放技能，压迫感就没了；只有贴着它翻滚、在抬手的半秒里判断格挡还是易武，神话的宏观才会落回到个体上。
《史记·夏本纪》里，禹治水是“与益、后稷奉帝命”，益还负责给百姓稻种；禹死后“以天下授益”，益又让位给启、退居箕山。
正史里的益是舜的虞官、禹的副手、和差一点接班的人，不是义子。游戏把他改成大禹的义子，是一次戏剧化压缩：君臣、搭档、继任者的复杂关系，被转成更容易进入的父子亲情，寻找失踪的义父给了玩家持续出发的理由
《淮南子·天文训》写得很清楚：“共工与颛顼争为帝，怒而触不周之山，天柱折，地维绝。天倾西北，故日月星辰移焉；地不满东南，故水潦尘埃归焉。”不周山不是普通的山，是天柱。天柱一断，天往西北塌，地往东南陷，水全往东南流——中国的地形和水系，在这段神话里被一次性解释了。
《山海经·大荒西经》说“有山而不合，名曰不周负子”。游戏叫《定海》，据点在“定海神珍铁”上。《西游记》第三回，龙王说这根铁是“大禹治水之时，定江海浅深的一个定子”。天柱断了，大禹就用一根“定子”去量江海的深浅——“定海”这个名字，本身就是“重新丈量世界”的意思。
一根断掉的天柱，一根用来定海的铁，叙事在这里就变得有趣起来。再加上一条原创的龙，整个游戏就变得非常饱满。
先秦两汉典籍里没有“炎帝麾下玄龙”这一号人物，但我们在游戏里看到一条龙作为主角总是觉得很合理。游戏把他写成炎帝麾下的大将，阪泉之战后遭夺名与放逐，绝地天通一役战死，数百年后以残魂和禁咒夺取益的肉身。
在上古叙事里，名字就是权力：赐姓、命氏、封号，都是把一个人编进秩序里的动作。炎帝赐他名，又剥夺他的名。至于夺舍，中国神话本来就有“借形”的传统：鲧化黄熊、女娃化精卫，都是死后变形；玄龙是反过来，用别人的形继续活。
这条命现在究竟算谁的？占据了躯壳的龙魂和化成羽嘉的人魂都有话说，玩家也想看到最后。
两把武器各占一组按键，不用按切换键。手柄上方块是近战普攻、三角是远程，L1/R1 是各自武技；连段中按另一把武器的攻击键，人物会顺势接一记“易武攻击”，无缝换手。弓的易武可以瞬间拉开距离，近战打完不必原地收招，远程被贴身也有回身反打的选择。玩家可以在剑的三段普攻后接弓的易武，把贴脸的怪推开；也可以在弓的滑步射后切回剑，抢一轮输出，这就让“打法切换”成为了一种必要的结合剂。除了标准的手柄支持之外，对于键鼠操作的支持也很妥帖。
兵器也是脾气分明。白宵剑以水化冰，寒圈缓速并削弱敌人，还保留格挡、招架；双刀放弃招架，靠攻速和闪避抢节奏；乌木弓的毒雾擅长区域消耗；飞雷弓用普攻积累、重击消耗；2.0 的断水双刃主打高频连击，武技累积连击后击出水属性伤害，并有概率生成冰柱。它鼓励你贪刀，而贪刀有代价——这套“风险换收益”的循环，是我觉得最像成熟动作游戏的地方。
打完一场战斗，场地中央会长出“聚宝树”，三选一，不满意可以消耗道具刷新。法宝分攻击、生存、奇诡、通用四类，游戏中共有两百多件，大多数还能进化。白宵剑的寒圈本来只是减攻击、减速，配上特定法宝可以打出眩晕，还能增加触发次数和伤害；乌木弓的毒雾则能进化成自动追击，或召唤会追人的“地毒虫”。几乎每一次有特定目标的选择，构筑的build都不同。
还记得我们前面说过的“定海神珍铁”么？游戏的据点建立于其上，也是合情合理。炼器台做装备、改武器，局内资源“地魄”一轮结束清零，“玄晶”能带回据点，配方和材料也不会全部蒸发。
这里就要说到游戏中的天赋树。它也分基础、绝式、近战武器技能、远程武器技能四支，也涉及装备栏位和聚宝树可选法宝数量。早期没点出关键天赋时，出招后被打断比较明显；天赋开放后，连招和容错会明显改善。永久成长适合扩充选择，不宜让玩家先忍受一段不必要的迟钝——至少新手阶段，应该更早让人尝到换武取消和连续闪避的甜头。
灵兽则是另一条线，收集碎片的过程并不算枯燥，打过BOSS后还有更多选择，失败了也给进度这点特别好，付出时间的尝试不是一无所获。
教学关最后的Boss是相柳。《山海经·海外北经》说它“九首，以食于九山”，禹杀相柳，“其血腥，不可以树五谷种”。游戏把它做成带蜈蚣身躯的巨兽，放在教学关当第一课——治水先杀神。它的体型很大，攻击多是大范围扫击，我依靠闪避的无敌帧钻过去；头多，视角经常被身体挡住，要靠声音和地面特效判断。
在2.0试玩版里，还多了许多游戏内容，比如玩家可以深入长年雷鸣不熄、天雷滚滚的全新关卡“河阳”，迎战另一位手持雷霆巨锤、富有压迫感和力量感的上古巨神“刑天”。整体游玩下来，各色boss的特色与不那么麻烦的重复游玩过程，倒让人觉得意犹未尽。
除了上面说到的相柳和刑天之外，还有修蛇、帝江这些Boss，虽然打多了功到自然成，但有时候还是需要小心驶得万年船。从Roguelike的角度上来说，《定海》有一定考验陌生玩家的因素在里面，但也没有垂直品类中一些追求顶尖难度的过分表达。
在2.0版本里，关卡是固定地图轮换，不是程序生成。节点路线可选，图标会提前标出下一区给的法宝类型；角落里藏着强化、素材、道具，只走主路会错过，这让支线探索也有了意义。
长线重复可玩性从当前来看值得进一步琢磨：五类武器两两组合、每把武器八种进化、两百多件法宝、灵兽技能组、天赋树、饰品炼器、隐藏 Boss、难度层级。在正式版本里现在可以继承 Demo 存档，也是承认了玩家已经付出的时间。对一款强调反复闯关的游戏，这比再添几句宣传口号实际。
2.0 之后，《定海》离正式版还有一段路。按官方说法，正式版会在 2026 年内推出。它现在的地基很扎实：动作手感在线，双武器有辨识度，法宝池够深，题材吃得透。
《山海经》对中国创作者的吸引力，在“未完成”。它条目式、碎片化、没有统一叙事，空白多，改编空间大。它是“地理书”而不是“故事书”，组织方式是空间的，天然适合关卡制游戏；同时它自带“博物学”的快感，收集、图鉴、分类，跟肉鸽的词条池是同一套心理机制。
这就是我对正式版最大的期待：让每一只BOSS，同时是一个关卡机制、一个流派核心、一段小传。几件事同时做到，《定海》就不只是“山海经题材的动作肉鸽”，而是“用动作游戏重写山海经”。
《定海》目前的版本给出的答案，是用动作来重新解读《山海经》里的洪荒史诗：通过动作，不断成长，搞定巨兽，敲定乾坤。

members.title: "It was crushing how hard it was" – The chaotic development of Dispatch, and what AdHoc Studio plans next

news.body:
"It was crushing how hard it was" – The chaotic development of Dispatch, and what AdHoc Studio plans next
CEO Michael Choung on getting a boost from Steam, the importance of caring about characters, and negotiating the funding wilderness
Today marks the one-year anniversary of the release of the first episode of Dispatch from AdHoc Studio, which went on to become one of the biggest surprise successes of 2025. Last November, the studio said Dispatch was on track to beat its three-year sales target after just three months.
The game has now been played by more than 5 million people, and a range of things has been organised to celebrate its anniversary. A new commentary and storyboard mode are being added to the deluxe edition of the game, a soundtrack vinyl set and book are being put together by Lost in Cult, a concert is planned in Los Angeles for December 3, and the game will launch on mobile on December 9.
But the celebrations were hard won. Michael Choung, CEO and co-founder of AdHoc, recalls that the game's release was a period of pandemonium, as the studio worked on each of the game's eight episodes right up to the last minute. "We thought we'd be done and we'd be cruising across the weekly releases, but it was not that at all," he tells GamesIndustry.biz.
Part of the problem was that the studio was still learning the ropes of self-publishing, dealing with things like console certification. "There were just a lot of things we were learning on the fly, and it was crushing how hard it was. And then on the other side of it, it blows up, and then it got busier. So all of this year has just been catching up to the success of the game and just trying to get it on as many platforms as possible. But it's been a wild, wild ride."
No one – apart, perhaps, from AdHoc itself – saw that success coming. Choung says that they talked to "everybody" in the publishing world, and no one was interested. The prevailing wisdom was that comedy and narrative-based games are a tough sell, and episodic has been a poisoned word in the industry for some time now.
"Everyone understood that these things don't make money, people don't buy these things. And so we literally talked to everyone. I've been at Gamescom the last four, five years, trying to scramble and find money from somewhere."
AdHoc was founded in 2019 by four Telltale alumni: Choung, Nick Herman, Dennis Lenart, and Pierre Shorette. Things seemed rosy at first. "We initially signed with a publisher, and they funded it up to a certain point," explains Choung. "Then maybe a third of the way they dropped us, essentially."
The studio had to scrabble together the remaining financing in the lead up to launch. Thankfully, after a trailer for Dispatch was shown at The Game Awards in December 2024, Critical Role stepped forward to offer some finishing funds, along with "a number of other partners," says Choung. Aside from that, AdHoc has made ends meet by taking on contract work.
"[AdHoc] was initially conceived as a work-for-hire studio, where we were just going to work on the narratives of other people's games," explains Choung. "We've actually kept that going, so there's always been that bit of work trickling in."
All in all, Choung describes the last couple of years as an incredibly chaotic time for the studio. "It's like a tornado occurred," he says – and the success of the game has only intensified that whirlwind. "It's like, oh, you think you're busy now? It's going to be much busier after this."
The secrets of success
When it comes to understanding exactly why Dispatch became so successful, Choung puts it down to how well the characters landed with audiences. In short, people cared about what happened to them.
"While we were at Telltale, I still remember one of the best pieces of feedback that we got, after the release of Tales from the Borderlands," Choung recalls. "It was someone saying, 'I want to keep playing this game because it feels like I'm just hanging out with my friends'."
Dispatch aimed for a similar vibe, using distinct characters with clear personalities. "People tend to remember everyone's name, which is something kind of rare, I think," says Choung. "And then there's so many characters that whatever you're into, whatever you're looking for in a relationship, it's kind of on offer or in some way, shape, or form."
He says that in an interactive narrative game like this, people tend to focus on how big the choices are in terms of their potential impact on how the game plays out, perhaps unlocking a completely different path or location. But really it comes down to the player's connection with the characters – any choice is big if it affects someone you care about.
"If you care about the characters, it matters a lot if you break a promise to somebody"
"The reality is that you have to actually care about the choices that you're making, it's not really the width of the choices that you're given. And the only way to make people care about that stuff is to just write compelling characters. If you care about the characters, it matters a lot if you break a promise to somebody or betray your friend. It's much smaller, much more relatable choices that I think are much more memorable and impactful."
"It's investment in those relationships and those characters, it's not how crazily the story changes based on the choices. Or I should say, it feels much bigger when you actually care about the characters, these small little choices that you're making."
Choung also credits streamers with helping Dispatch to reach a big audience. "We didn't know how friendly it was for streamers," he says. "You can pause at a choice and talk to your audience about, 'Oh my gosh, what's going on?'" He adds that people who had played the game already would go back and watch their favourite streamer play through it to see what choices they made.
Steam gave Dispatch a big leg up, too – which is where the episodic structure helped. Choung says Dispatch was on the front page of Steam "in some way, shape, or form" for the entire time between the release of the first episode on October 22 and the launch of the final one on November 12.
"That accounts for hundreds of millions of impressions," he says. "It was one of those things where they called us last minute, and they were like, 'Hey, we want to [do a] test. If we put this on the front page for your wishlisters, we want to see if they'll respond and if it'll do well. And if it does, then maybe we can have a conversation about putting it on the front page for everybody'. Four hours later, it was on the front page for everybody. That was the big sort of early momentum, and then everything else came afterwards: the influencers, the creators, all that stuff."
He says it's a testament to the levelling power of the games industry, and how it diverges from Hollywood. "Games like ours can sit next to a $200 million shooter and no one bats an eye."
Lessons learned
AdHoc might now be basking in success, but it was tough road. Looking back, Choung says there are some things he might have done differently.
"We took longer than we needed to," he says. "I mean, for instance, we had an animation test pretty early that we shelved. We had this project pretty early, and we shelved it, I think two different times. We were like, 'Ah, let's go explore some other stuff'. And if we hadn't have done that, that means we would've spent more time on the game, so maybe it would've been better.
"But the reality is our approach is one that requires us to reexamine things constantly, and that can be tiresome at times. But I think ultimately the end result is something that feels like it's hitting a bar that no one else has really aimed at."
"We made basically three feature-length movies and a video game on top of each other. That's what we did. We literally did not know that that's what we were signing up for."
The animation in Dispatch was done by Igloo in Thailand, with AdHoc sending over storyboards for the studio. But inevitably, AdHoc would sometimes come back to Igloo with suggested tweaks to the animation once it was done. "I feel like we did a pretty good job, but yeah, we absolutely changed stuff," says Choung. "There's always something that can be better."
The future
Looking ahead, Choung says AdHoc will "definitely" pursue an episodic release model again, adding that the number of concurrent players "essentially just kept doubling" every time AdHoc released a new episode of Dispatch. He thinks the regular weekly release schedule helped: the studio was at pains to avoid the "irregular" episode drops under Telltale, which he acknowledges were "super frustrating".
There's also the possibility of taking Dispatch to film and TV. "It's definitely something that we're interested in," says Choung, adding that Dmitri M. Johnson from Story Kitchen has been in touch, "among others".
But right now, he and the rest of AdHoc are just glad to have a chance to catch their breath after a roller-coaster couple of years. That said, they still have an eye on the future. "There are conversations about what's next for sure. I don't think we've hard-committed to anything just yet, but there's definitely more in store," he says.
"The studio is focused on original IP, and we want to make original stories," he adds. "We kind of screwed ourselves with Dispatch because it's so big, you can't ignore it. You can't walk away from it necessarily. But we want to tell all kinds of different stories.
"I think right now we're still at that phase where there's so many options, it's really hard to narrow down into one specific thing. But I'm sure soon enough – and we have to make a call really, really soon – we'll be announcing something."

news.title: Meeting you where you work: Inside 200M+ Unity CLI events
news.summary_raw: Unity CLI usage data from 200 million events: 98% of runs come from AI coding agents and automation. See the top commands, agents, and where it’s used.

members.title: Meeting you where you work: Inside 200M+ Unity CLI events

news.body:
Meeting you where you work: Inside 200M+ Unity CLI events
Christopher Addison - Unity
Developers start in the agent they already use, in the editor they already like, with the terminal they already have open. The Unity CLI meets you there. It’s a single binary that installs and manages Unity from the terminal and, with the Pipeline package, drives a running Editor, so scripts, CI, and coding agents all reach Unity the same way.
Since July, more than 226,000 logged-in users have used the Unity CLI, and it has logged more than 200 million events (and growing). Almost all of them are commands being run. What those commands show is a simple habit: people set Unity up, then their agent does the work.
People set it up, then hand it off
From July 20 to October 13, 2026, about 98% of CLI runs come from coding agents and other automation. People typing at a terminal account for 0.2%, and CI pipelines for 0.3%. A small share of runs falls outside those three groups.
When people do type, they are getting ready. They install the Pipeline package, open a project on the right Editor version, sign in, point their agent at Unity, and install the CLI skill. Then they hand the work over. That is what meeting developers where they work looks like in practice: Unity shows up inside the agent they already chose, and the agent takes it from there.
Most of the work happens inside a live Editor
The three commands run most:
unity command
about 124 million runs: runs a command on a connected Editor, either a built-in one or one you defined yourself.unity status
about 6.7 million: shows the live state of every connected Editor, including its project and version.unity pipeline list
about 1.4 million: lists Editor instances and whether each one has the Pipeline package.
Unity’s plugins bring official skills to agents
Most of the CLI's usage came after Unity released official plugins for Claude Code and Codex, and most recently, Grok. Each plugin gives the agent skills written by Unity's own teams, including one that drives the CLI, so the agent works in Unity the way Unity intends. unity setup claude
installs the Claude Code plugin for you, and the plugin also works in the Claude Code extension for VS Code. Agents that are not integrated with Unity’s official plugin can still work in Unity through the CLI, so you keep the agent you already use.
Claude Code is the agent used most with the CLI, followed by Codex, then other agents such as Cursor and Grok. The rest come from scripts and tools that do not identify an agent.
Where it is being used
By signed-in users, the CLI's largest audiences are in the United States, Japan, and South Korea, followed by Germany.
What’s next
We will keep adding agents, and keep publishing what we learn. To get started, see the Unity CLI documentation and the Unity plugin documentation.
How we measured this
All CLI figures come from Unity CLI's aggregated telemetry, July 20 to October 13, 2026, with Unity employees excluded. Developers who opt out are not counted. Each event is counted once, so retries do not inflate the totals. Country is based on the location attached to each event, and some events carry no location. The split between agents, CI, and people covers July 20 to October 13, 2026. A run counts as CI when a x`CI environment variable is set, and as a person when both input and output are a terminal. Runs in MCP mode, runs from a known AI tool, and other piped or scripted runs count as agents and automation.

news.title: Skipping domain reload: faster iteration using the MethodReload feature
news.summary_raw: Stop waiting on domain reloads! Learn how MethodReload speeds up Unity iteration time, explore its limitations, and compare it to existing hot reload tools.

members.title: Skipping domain reload: faster iteration using the MethodReload feature

news.body:
Skipping domain reload: faster iteration using the MethodReload feature
We've all been there: you tweak some gameplay code and then wait for the Editor to complete a domain reload. The process can slow down your iteration time and really drain your creativity. Not to mention the extra time spent iterating on a device, where each cycle requires a full build.
Our answer to this is MethodReload. We demoed it on stage at Unite Seoul and it is available now as an experimental package. In this post we’ll cover how to use MethodReload, what its limitations are, and how it compares to hot reload tools you may already have in your project.
Why we're stuck reloading
A little history helps here, because the reason domain reload exists is also the reason it's hard to get rid of.
Play Mode was built on Mono's AppDomains where code changes kicked off a familiar process: tear down the domain, load the new assemblies, re-JIT, and then resume in the same process. For years that was a genuine superpower, and it's a big part of why iterating in Unity felt fast compared to building a player.
It's also a blunt instrument, meaning that during the reload everything goes away and everything comes back, whether you changed one method or one hundred. Furthermore, IL2CPP doesn’t support domain reloads at all, so every change requires rebuilding the entire player.
You might be asking yourself, “won't CoreCLR fix this?” and the answer is: Not magically. While CoreCLR does away with domain reloads, it still has to reload assemblies, and MethodReload can help here as well.
How to use MethodReload
As mentioned above, MethodReload is available now and it ships in com.unity.pipeline
, currently at 0.7.0-exp.1
.
The process of using MethodReload is fairly simple. Just tag one or more methods with the [MethodReload]
attribute, start the watcher, enter Play Mode or attach a development player, and then edit the body of your methods. The running instance picks up the new body on its next call.
MethodReload doesn't replace domain reloads completely, however. Bigger changes still go through the usual compile. But for the small tweaks that make up most of an iteration loop, it turns a long wait into a matter of seconds, in the Editor and on device alike.
Try it out
The fastest way to understand MethodReload is to run it, so if you’d like to test this out yourself, here are some steps to get you started. Note: since this is an experimental feature, the process may change in the future and be different from what is described here
1. Install the package (Unity 6.0+ required). You can either install it through the Unity CLI or use the Package Manager to add the Pipeline package manually using “Install package by technical name” and this string: com.unity.pipeline@0.7.0-exp.1
.
2. Tag the methods you iterate on. The attribute has to be there before you enter Play Mode or build a player, because the dispatch check is woven in at compile time. Tagged methods must be public
(instance or static) and return void
or IEnumerator
; anything else is skipped at build time with a warning.
using Unity.Pipeline.MethodReload;
using UnityEngine;
public class Spinner : MonoBehaviour
{
public float rotationSpeed = 90f;
[MethodReload]
public void Update()
{
transform.Rotate(Vector3.up, rotationSpeed * Time.deltaTime);
}
}
3. Start the watcher. In order for your MethodReload to see your changes live, you will need to start the MethodReload Watcher. Do this by going to Project Settings → Pipeline → Editor, then in the “Method Reload Interpreter Watch” section, click Start Watching.
While the watcher covers the whole Assets tree, a saved .cs
only compiles if it contains a MethodReload
attribute, so unrelated saves cost you nothing.
4. If testing in the editor: enter Play Mode. Once running, any tagged code change will be compiled and injected in place. Once you leave play mode, your changes will compile and go through the usual domain reload.
5. If testing on device: plug in a device. Build a development player with the runtime Pipeline driver enabled. Connect the device with Autoconnect Profiler, or attach through the Profiler or Console window. From then on, every save compiles in the Editor using the player's preprocessor defines and pushes to every connected player. No restart is needed in either direction.
Two workflow details worth knowing up front:
- Auto-refresh is off while the watcher runs, so a save reloads instead of triggering a domain reload; other assets won't import until you hit Ctrl/Cmd+R, and Stop Watching puts your settings back.
- The watch survives domain reloads: it re-applies edits that a Play Mode reload wiped, and re-pushes to a player that reconnects, since a restarted player boots the original compiled code.
What about using the CLI?
If you prefer working in a terminal, want to work through an agent, or want to push every tagged method rather than only what changed since the watch started, the same functionality is exposed as Unity CLI commands:
# Reload in the Editor through the interpreter
unity command reload_file_editor_interpreter "Assets/Scripts/Spinner.cs"
# Compile in the Editor, push to connected players (folders work too)
unity command reload_file_player_interpreter "Assets/Scripts" --player 2
Limitations
There's no way around domain reload without compromises, and the limitations on MethodReload are in three places: what kinds of change it can apply, what C# it can run, and how fast it runs.
Only tagged method bodies change. A reload never touches call sites, fields, or type layout. No new fields, no new classes. That constraint is what makes it safe to apply to a live instance, and it's the one you plan around: decide which methods you'll be iterating on and tag them. A reload can declare a new method and call it from a reloaded body, but that method can't be a reload entry point, because nothing compiled knows to call it until your next real compile.
It runs a C# subset. The interpreter is hand-built and has to stay small enough to live inside a player, so it doesn't implement all of C#. Inside a [MethodReload]
body you cannot use:
await
andTask
,try
/catch
/finally
,lock
, LINQ query syntax,checked
decimal
,dynamic
, reflection types, threading typesref
,out
, andin
parameters,ref
returns and locals, multi-dimensional arrays (jagged is fine), generic methods
What does work covers most gameplay code : primitives, method calls, loops, delegates, string interpolation, coroutine yield
, collections. A Roslyn analyzer ships with the package and flags violations in your IDE, on tagged bodies only, so you find out while typing rather than after a push.
On device, interpreted code can only call what the player exposes. IL2CPP strips code with no references, so a reloaded body that calls a UnityEngine or BCL member your build never used has nothing to call. In the Editor, missing members bind on demand. On a device, the push checks up front and lists missing members as warnings; if the code reaches one anyway, it throws an exception. Rule of thumb: change what a method does, not the set of APIs it depends on.
Interpreted code is slower than compiled code. That's the nature of an interpreter, whether the comparison is IL2CPP ahead of time or Mono and CoreCLR just in time. It only affects tagged methods in development builds. In release builds there is no prologue and no interpreter; a tagged method just runs its compiled body. Ultimately, it is up to you to decide if the performance hit during iteration is worth the improved iteration speed and convenience.
Coroutines pick up changes at creation. A [MethodReload] IEnumerator
method uses the new body the next time StartCoroutine
runs. Coroutines already in flight keep the body they started with. Pair it with [OnMethodReloaded]
, a parameterless instance method that fires on every live instance after a reload lands on its type, and you have a domain-reload-free OnEnable
for restarting long-lived loops:
[OnMethodReloaded]
void OnMethodReloaded()
{
StopAllCoroutines();
StartCoroutine(MainLoop());
}
How it works under the hood
It's the combination of two ideas: the first is that compiling C# produces IL bytecode, and IL that stays inside a modest subset can be executed by an interpreter instead of being compiled. That interpreter is itself ordinary C#, so IL2CPP compiles it along with the rest of your game, which is what lets it run on device.
The second idea is getting into it. Every [MethodReload]
method has a wired path to the interpreter. Branching to the interpreter is done by weaving a prologue in the tagged methods at compile time. Decompiled, it looks like this:
[MethodReload]
public void TakeDamage(int amount)
{
// weaved during compilation
if (MethodReloadRegistry.HasOverride("Player.TakeDamage") &&
MethodReloadRegistry.TryInvokeMethodReload(
"Player.TakeDamage", this, amount))
{
return;
}
// initial code
hp -= amount;
}
The woven check asks the registry whether an override exists for this method. The watcher and the CLI fill that registry with freshly compiled IL. If there's an entry, the interpreter runs it and the original body is skipped. Otherwise the compiled code runs as usual.
How this compares
Good tools already exist for iterating on C# without a domain reload, and we'd rather be precise about where each applies than pretend they don't.
Packages from the Asset Store patch methods in a running Mono runtime. That gives them an excellent Editor experience, full C# in the reloaded body, no tagging step, and in Hot Reload's case an on-device mode for Mono player builds. All real advantages. It also means that they don’t work with an IL2CPP player because there's no runtime to patch.
.NET Hot Reload, the feature in Visual Studio and Rider for .NET applications, applies edits through the runtime's edit-and-continue path. It's built for CoreCLR and doesn't target Unity's Mono or IL2CPP runtimes.
MethodReload sits in a different spot with its interpreter backend trading language coverage

news.summary_raw: The 2026 Epic AI MegaJam runs November 12–15. Team up with up to four other humans and as many AI agents as you want to build a playable game in Unreal Engine or UEFN, and compete for cash prizes.
news.rss_content: The 2026 Epic AI MegaJam runs November 12–15. Team up with up to four other humans and as many AI agents as you want to build a playable game in Unreal Engine or UEFN, and compete for cash prizes.

members.title: Vibe your way to $50k: the 2026 Epic AI MegaJam is coming

news.body:
The 2026 Epic AI MegaJam starts on November 12. Team with up to four other humans and unlimited agents to build a playable game in Unreal Engine or Unreal Editor for Fortnite (UEFN), and compete for cash prizes.
Jam online from anywhere, with your local game dev community, or in person in San Francisco at Digital Jungle, where you’ll build alongside teams from Anthropic, Google, Meshy, OpenAI, SpaceXSI, and more.
Bring any AI tools into your workflow, from asset generation to coding agents. Get creative! Prototype the mechanic you never had time for, or try the art style you weren’t sure you could pull off.
Kickoff livestream. Tune in on November 11 at 11 AM PST / 2 PM EST on Twitch, YouTube, and X for the theme reveal, jam details, and special guests.
Four days to build. The jam runs November 12–15. Work on your project starts November 12.
Two days in person. Join us November 14-15 at Digital Jungle in San Francisco. In-person registration opens on November 1 at 7 AM PST / 10 AM EST. Spots are limited.
Daily livestreams. Tune in at 11 AM PST / 2 PM EST each day of the jam for tips, progress updates, and a look at what developers are building, or watch on demand on Youtube.
Cash prizes. Winners in every category take home cash from Epic Games.
Sponsored prizes. Some of our AI partners are giving jammers credits to build with their tools. Stay tuned for more.
Categories and prizes
Each submission can win one main category and one modifier category. Prizes are subject to the Official Rules, and eligibility restrictions apply. For details, check out the 2026 AI MegaJam itch.io page.
Main categories
Best Overall, Unreal Engine: $7,500 for first place, $5,000 for second place, and $2,500 for third place
Best Overall, UEFN: $7,500 for first place, $5,000 for second place, and $2,500 for third place
Best Student Project (Unreal Engine or UEFN): $7,500 for first place, $5,000 for second place, and $2,500 for third place
Development Continuation Grants
Standout Unreal Engine and UEFN entries can earn development continuation grants of up to $50,000 to keep building after the jam, so the momentum doesn’t stop when the jam ends.
Modifier categories
Best Team: best overall team, $5,000
Solo Driver: best game built by a solo developer, $2,500
Render Royalty: best overall visuals, photoreal or stylized, $2,500
Pocket Powerhouse: best mobile game, with one Unreal Engine and one UEFN winner, $2,500 each
Glass Box: best dev log showing how you built your game, $2,500
Walkie-Talkie: best narrative-driven UEFN game featuring LLM-powered NPCs and characters built with conversations, $2,500
Get ready to jam
The jam starts November 12, so now’s the time to gather your team, set up your agentic coding tools, and get comfortable with Model Context Protocol (MCP) before kickoff. Here are a few resources to help you get started.

news.title: 认真肝了30个小时之后, 我被《三国志：霸王崛起》打脸了
news.summary_raw: 资深三国SLG玩家实测《三国志：霸王崛起》封测30小时，从美术、玩法、节奏、社交、付费等维度评测，梳理亮点与不足，给出游玩参考。

members.title: 认真肝了30个小时之后, 我被《三国志：霸王崛起》打脸了

news.body:
先说身份：率土四年、三战两年、三谋开服玩到现在，市面上的三国SLG我基本没落下过。
老玩家看新品，眼光是刁的——题材早就卷烂了，武将立绘一个比一个精美，但真正能在玩法上拿出新东西的，这些年数不出几个。
10月13日《三国志：霸王崛起》烽火测试开服，我当天进的服，三天肝了30多个小时，发展度冲到22万+。删档测试的号不值得投入太多感情，但正好可以放开手脚把各个系统都试一遍。
所以这篇文章就回答一个问题：三国SLG已经卷成这样，这款新品到底能不能打？
一、题材与美术：三国味正不正
进游戏第一感觉：走的是3D写实路线，味是正的。
大地图以道路连接名城，历史著名古战场被做成了必争的卡点，山川关隘的排布看得出是照着三国地理逻辑来的，不是随便画一张皮。
武将人设没有搞魔改那一套，关羽还是关羽，诸葛亮还是诸葛亮。立绘是写实偏国风的风格，盔甲兵器看得出参考了汉代形制，不是网游风的浮夸堆砌。战斗演出中规中矩，技能释放有专属动画，配乐用了大量鼓点和民乐，攻城战的氛围渲染到位。
小吐槽一句：主界面UI图标偏多，前期各种功能红点轮番轰炸，信息密度对新手不太友好，希望公测版能再收敛一点。
二、核心玩法：策略深度够不够
这是全文重点，也是这款游戏真正不一样的地方。
先说最大的差异点：它把传统SLG的"铺路"拿掉了。大地图通行以道路连接名城为底层逻辑，行军不用再一格一格铺过去。这个改动看似是减负，实际带来的连锁反应很有意思——绝大多数城池被移到了道路两侧，不再生硬地挡住你的行军路线，只有历史古战场作为卡点扼守要冲。这意味着你可以选择在敌后广阔地带来一场"孤军深入"，但也必须时刻盯着地图：敌人可能在某个隐蔽的岔路口修一座"坞堡"或"要塞"，直接切断你的退路。
要塞和坞堡是这作的原创沙盘建筑，玩家自由落子，可以改变道路通行规则、支援城池防御、锁敌咽喉。实测下来，这套"动态道路"设计让地图博弈的密度明显高了一档：每一次行军都像在下棋，你堵别人的时候，别人也在算你的后路。
第二个差异点是阵营设计。游戏共设6大阵营，除了玩家可选择的三大势力，还有三个由独立AI驱动的NPC阵营跟玩家结盟。注意，这些AI不是送资源的工具人——官方的说法是它们有自己的"战略目标"，会自主判断是否出兵增援、是否坚守，甚至在利益面前可能让你的部队先上去蹚雷。封测阶段我还没完全摸透AI的行为逻辑，但"盟友不一定靠得住"这个设定，确实把外交博弈的权重拉高了。
武将养成这块，职业体系+缘分机制的组合也有纵深：同职业上阵有专属加成，配队不是无脑堆数值；赠送酒水这类亲密度道具可以提升武将缘分等级、解锁专属羁绊，同一个武将可以养出完全不同的方向。技能方面，武将可以拆解传承战法，主力武将的技能槽要靠战法点慢慢喂——我的陆逊把"风助火势"换成了S级战法"士别三日"，输出直接上了一个档次。
开荒配队也不用自己瞎摸，游戏内置了阵容推荐，开荒期的"蔡琰骑"这种平民组合直接给出一键应用，前排顶住、后排群体输出，前期开荒推图基本无损。我自己的主力是陆逊、司马懿、周瑜的智将组合，群体伤害推关很顺。
槽点也说一个：系统多、机制新，但部分玩法的说明文案偏简略，围城值攻城这类新机制的实际规则要靠自己打几场才摸明白，新手期容易走弯路。
三、成长节奏与新手引导
制作人在开发者的话里明确说了，这款游戏的初衷就是解决"太累"的问题——无止境的铺路、半夜被沦陷的挫败感，都是他们想砍掉的负担。
实测感受基本对得上这个承诺：不铺路，个人基地绝对安全，不会被半夜偷家。新手保护期给得也实在——占领读条只要9秒、打资源点体力消耗减半、夜晚功能随天数逐步开放，发育期的心理压力小了很多。
行动消耗统一走"策令"，屯田、劫掠、攻城、讨伐都花它，每小时自然恢复1个。这个设计等于给肝度上了硬限：想爆肝也没地方使力，节奏被系统帮你卡住了。
资源获取也不抠门。开服活动"技能升华"跟着任务走就能拿金铢和战法点，第1天熟悉发育循环和开荒节奏，第3天前后阵营战等核心玩法陆续开放，节奏卡点卡得比较准。
世界频道从开服第一天就很热闹，问配队的、喊组队的、军团红包招人的都有，新游戏的社区氛围起来了。
对观望玩家最关心的问题——"怕复杂、怕肝、怕逼氪"——就封测体验来看，护肝这一条是做到了；系统虽多但分步解锁，中度玩家理解成本可控。
四、社交与军团：长线耐不耐玩
阵营制SLG的社交结构天然比散人局更紧密，这作把这一点放大了。
攻城采用"围城值"机制，不是单纯拼战力的对撞，集结、围城的节奏需要军团统一调度。军团界面里贡献、军功、战报、日志一应俱全，沙盘议事厅的仪式感做得挺足。加上AI阵营这个变量存在，军团外交不再只是玩家之间的合纵连横，怎么"用"好AI盟友、怎么防着被AI盟友算计，都是指挥层要操心的新课题。
服务器里军团招人已经卷起来了，红包、军费、福利明码标价地刷——这在SLG里是好兆头，说明核心那批策略玩家认这个产品。以封测内容推测，赛季制的长线空间是有的，但具体赛季规则还要等官方进一步披露。
五、付费体验：逼不逼氪
直接说体感：付费点主要集中在武将招募、月卡战令和成长礼包这几类常规设计上，礼包档位从1元、6元到30元，没有冒出什么出格的新花样。
关键看零氪微氪的生存空间。我全程只充了一张月卡，发育节奏没有明显被卡脖子，开荒推图靠蔡琰这类易获取的武将够用，和头部玩家的差距主要体现在进度快慢，而不是能不能玩。
客观讲，这套付费设计在同类里处于中间水位——不是最良心的那一档，但也谈不上逼氪。具体如何，建议公测后自己进去感受两天再判断。
结尾：值不值得玩
总结一下：
亮点三条——无铺路+动态道路的沙盘革新，地图博弈密度高；AI同盟阵营设计，外交策略有纵深；武将职业+缘分机制，配队养将不枯燥。
不足两条——前期UI信息密度偏高；新机制说明不够清晰，上手有摸索成本。
整体评价：超出预期，值得一试。策略老炮能吃到动态沙盘和阵营外交的深度，三国粉能吃到题材红利，被传统SLG"肝"怕了的玩家，可以把它当作一次低负担的回归尝试。它未必能颠覆谁，但在2026年还在认真琢磨"SLG怎么减负又不失深度"的新品里，这一款是想明白了的。
最后，评论区开放提问：还想了解哪个系统，留言告诉我，我去游戏里帮大家试。

news.summary_raw: 在巴黎游戏周前夕，游戏将以一套趣味外观，向法国游戏创意精神致敬

members.title: 致敬法国创意精神 《雷曼：传奇再叙》全新“法棍”外观公布

news.body:
中国，上海– 2026年10月22日 –今日，育碧宣布《雷曼：传奇再叙》将在发售时同步推出的全新外观，为这场经典平台跳跃冒险再添一份法式幽默。
全新“法棍”外观将同时适用于雷曼与芭芭拉。它将以轻松诙谐的方式，向另一款诞生于法国蒙彼利埃的游戏佳作致敬。作为法国工作室之间的一次献礼，这套外观所赞颂的那份创造力、热情以及独具一格的法式风情，正是让法国电子游戏产业始终在国际舞台上大放异彩的真正特质。
凭借独特的夸张外观与诙谐的气质，“法棍”外观体现了长久以来构成雷曼系列核心特色的幽默、魅力与匠心。同时也以含蓄的方式，致敬了一部在开发团队心中占据特殊地位的作品。
“这不是一幅画，这是现实！”自《雷曼：传奇再叙》发售首日起，玩家即可让雷曼与芭芭拉穿上“法棍”外观展开冒险，为《雷曼：传奇再叙》的奇幻世界之旅再添一抹独特的本土风味。
《雷曼：传奇再叙》将于2026年12月3日登陆 PlayStation 5、Nintendo Switch 2、Xbox Series X|S 以及 PC 平台（包括育碧商城及Steam）。届时，所有玩家皆可免费获取“法棍”外观。
由育碧蒙彼利埃与育碧米兰联合领衔开发的《雷曼：传奇再叙》，是对这款广受好评的平台跳跃游戏的全新演绎，加入了全新内容与情节转折。玩家将体验快节奏动作、史诗冒险、欢乐混乱与缤纷惊喜。
玩家既可以独自踏上冒险，也可以与家人、朋友一同挑战关卡。游戏支持最多四人本地合作，进化后的“功夫足球”模式也将回归，让大家在轻松热闹的对抗中创造难忘的欢乐时刻。

news.title: Opinion: Why words matter when we prioritize 'core teams' in game development
news.summary_raw: How we describe game development will inevitably shape our processes.

members.title: Opinion: Why words matter when we prioritize 'core teams' in game development

news.body:
Opinion: Why words matter when we prioritize 'core teams' in game development
How we describe game development will inevitably shape our processes.
A recent social media dustup in the game development community has given the industry reason to scrutinize the phrase "core team." Said dustup occurred after Gamesindustry.biz published an in-depth story breaking down the "distributed development" model that Fuse Games employed in the making of Star Wars: Galactic Racer. Said model divides the development team into three categories centered around a "core team."
It's a useful framework for describing a complex method for creating games that require hundreds of developers to bring across the finish line—so why did a number of developers express frustration over a Bluesky post from the outlet (disclaimer—I was among those voicing such a reaction) that stated "Star Wars: Galactic Racer was made by a core team of 75 people"?
It's a valid question—one that takes on more weight when you realize how many studios are establishing development practices similar to Fuse's distributed development model. The answer comes down to how you interpret the phrase "was made by," as a similar sentence appears in the story itself.
The statement is factually true as Fuse Games' core team often consisted of fewer than 75 people during development. But is is also not true, as the game was truly made by roughly 1,100 people who appear in the game's credits. One could interpret the phrase as a neutral descriptor of the "core team"—but one could also interpret it as obscuring the work of the hundreds of developers who helped bring us the viral delight that is Biddy Blas.
It's intended to be the former. GI.biz features editor Lewis Packwood confirmed as much to me in an email exchange this week, where he pointed out the phrase "core" is a word Webster used to refer to the team at Fuse Games. "Both his comments and the article made clear that Galactic Racer was the work of many different people in different places, not just the 75 staff at Fuse Games," he explained. "Given that this model of a small full-time team directing and coordinating a range of external companies is relatively new to the games industry, it may just be that we haven't yet developed the proper language to adequately describe it."
Packwood (who deserves a tip of the cap for participating in this inadvertent exercise in public editing) has absolutely nailed what made the post divisive: the still-germinating "proper language" for describing this game development process. And that doesn't invalidate the distress of the veteran developers who've made Bluesky their collective watering hole.
The reaction spotlights why we need precise communication when describing the realities of game development—because history shows that when we boil the success of a game down to the work of a few individuals, we can literally devalue developers, and potentially erode their careers.
In-groups and out-groups already devalue developers
The phrase "core team" is a slippery term, as it has no institutional definition and circles close to concepts of in-groups and out-groups that already plague game development. You could become a core team member by being friends with the company founders or going through a long and arduous job application process. You can be excluded because of your job title, your interpersonal relationships, or in the worst case, your race, gender, or sexuality.
The phrase also comes with political and financial weight. We hear often about how core teams from large studios become the ones who secure funding for new startups. They're often the last ones left after studios lay workers off in the wake of an unsuccessful game. One investor I spoke with at DICE explained that when taking pitches, he prioritizes the strength of the core team because no matter how many employees a company hires or lays off, that's the group he expects to adapt to the changes and bring a game across the finish line.
At best, core teams are amazing groups of colleagues who work well and have learned how to communicate with each other. At worst, they're cliques of senior and lead developers taking credit for other employees' work, sometimes shielded from the consequences of bad behavior by their close relationships with the central group. This even bleeds into the world of distributed development, where external developers are sometimes barred from speaking with members of the "core team" or even publicizing that they worked on a given game.
That dynamic is one reason why some developers (particularly American ones, it seems) flinch at a future built on distributed development.
When done right, the model diversifies financial risk and preserves what works about triple-A development without the need to keep everyone under one corporate entity. When done wrong, you can wind up with a game development class system, where creative direction and funding flows in limited directions, and those not lucky enough to be at the center struggle to keep doing the work they love.
This problem is obviously organizational in nature, and not easily fixed by good copyediting. But organizations begin with language, and the language we use to define our work will define the future of video game development.
How should we describe distributed development?
So how do we define the "proper language" of distributed development? Let's dig into what made this simple sentence such a point of contention: my old enemy, that dreaded demon, the passive voice.
This devilish grammatical construction is my main adversary as an editor at GameDeveloper.com. Unlike the active voice, it obscures agency over the subject of a sentence. Compare "Star Wars: Galactic Racer was made by a core team of 75" to "a core team of 75 made Galactic Racer." One sentence has the ring of truth. The other drifts dangerously close to falsehood.
If I were to say "Fuse Games developed Star Wars: Galactic Racer," I would be communicating a fact that doesn't obscure the work of other teams. The game industry broadly recognizes that when you say a studio develops a game, all the partner studios are subsidiary to the one listed as "developer" on the storefront. If I needed to elaborate, I might write "Fuse Games employed a 'distributed model,' where a core team of 75 developers recruited a collection of co-dev, exdev, and outsourcing partners to distribute the financial risk of building a game with hundreds of employees."
But I can feel my editorial director Alissa McAloon simmering in the corner, as we have regularly debated the use of passive voice in articles. So if we were to preserve the technique, we might say "Galactic Racer was developed by Fuse Games, which recruited a collection of co-dev, exdev, and outsourcing partners to support a core team of 75 employees."
Is all this just nitpicking? Perhaps. But this whole incident reminded me of when Game Awards founder Geoff Keighley took the stage at Summer Game Fest 2025 and sung the praises of Sandfall Interactive and Kepler Interactive's Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, saying that the game comes "a team of under 30 developers who bravely stepped away from big publishers to forge their own path."
Over 500 people worked on Clair Obscur in one form or another. Around 470 of those people weren't necessarily working on the game in a full-time capacity or were present for much of the development cycle. But the 50 million people who watched Summer Game Fest won't know that distinction.
With one sentence, Keighley may have inadvertently told the audience whose work on the game mattered, and whose was incidental. We don't need to do the same.

news.title: Terraforming The Alters: Last Variable with Blender, ZBrush & UE5
news.summary_raw: Artem Ostapchuk of 11 bit studios shared how the team built the terraforming pipeline for The Alters: Last Variable, visualizing alien flora over a barren planet with opaque Nanite cutout geometry, PCG scattering and a global HISM system so every level worked in both its scorched and terraformed states.

members.title: Terraforming The Alters: Last Variable with Blender, ZBrush & UE5

news.body:
Terraforming The Alters: Last Variable with Blender, ZBrush & UE5
Artem Ostapchuk of 11 bit studios shared how the team built the terraforming pipeline for The Alters: Last Variable, visualizing alien flora over a barren planet with opaque Nanite cutout geometry, PCG scattering and a global HISM system so every level worked in both its scorched and terraformed states.
Introduction
Hello everyone! My name is Artem Ostapchuk, and I’m a Senior 3D Environment Artist at 11 bit studios. You might have seen my previous breakdown here on 80 Level about my Japanese Shinto Shrine personal project. Today, I’m back to share a look behind the scenes of environment work on The Alters: Last Variable DLC, focusing on the pipeline of filling our levels with lush vegetation under real production constraints.
Base Game vs. The DLC
On the base game of The Alters, I was responsible for building environment pipelines across several acts, creating meshes, materials, and internal tools - from anomaly-twisted canyons to interdimensional foliage veins only visible with a specialized flashlight. The main game's world was defined by its harsh, barren desolation, where players race to survive a planet-scorching sun.
In the Last Variable DLC, the story expands into terraforming. The environment had to work seamlessly in both its original barren state and its newly overgrown, terraformed version. My main focus was putting together the terraforming pipeline – making the foliage sets, landscape layers, master materials, a few helper tools, and dressing several areas across the levels.
Designing the Flora: Accelerated Growth
We wanted the vegetation to feel alien without falling into generic sci-fi tropes or looking like everyday Earth plants. Our narrative concept was simple: fossilized trees and dead alien soil get hit with a powerful terraforming liquid, triggering explosive, unnatural growth. This gave us a distinct visual language based on heavy moss accumulation, lots of branch structures, and coral-like vegetation spreading across the rock and trees.
References & The Beauty Corner
Working from the initial concept by Robert Rejmak, we gathered references and built a dedicated "beauty corner" – a small test scene where we could test the assets, shaders, and terrain blending. Finding references was easy, it's incredible how many strange plants there are on our planet, and that was more than enough inspiration to ground our alien flora in a believable way.
Moving from base game to DLC, our core software stack stayed mostly the same: Blender and ZBrush for modeling and sculpting organic forms, and Substance 3D Designer & Painter for texturing.
For all our foliage, we relied exclusively on opaque Nanite meshes. That means no transparency – every small leaf and grass blade is actual cutout geometry. In our benchmark tests, this performed much better than using traditional masked shaders, so we went with that approach. Several assets also feature subtle World Position Offset (WPO) wind animation driven by vertex color channels – a technique I covered in more detail in my previous 80 Level breakdown.
As a team of three environment artists (with Patrycja Kusińska and Krzysztof Knysak), we each took ownership of different areas, so цу used additional tools like SpeedTree or Houdini depending on the specific task. I also like to use spline- and weight-based methods to spawn meshes in Blender's geometry nodes; it's a quick, artist-friendly way to create foliage assets.
And for landscape, like in the original game, we used VHM/RVT instead of Nanite landscape.
We didn't have a fixed schedule for making meshes. With only a few concepts and level designs constantly changing, we built the foliage kit on the fly and tested what worked and what didn't. The beauty corner we did early on gave us a clear picture of what we were aiming for, so whenever the spaces changed, we just added whatever new pieces were needed to make them work.
Designing for Scale & Custom In-Engine Tools
Since we didn't use the Houdini Engine/Live Link bridge directly into Unreal, we relied entirely on in-engine tools to scatter and populate the levels with flora. I created a few tools that greatly helped us with this task: PCG mesh scattering, geometry-script moss generation, and trace-based scattering. That helped us deliver a big overgrown world in a short time. We've also massively used level instances – reusing what's already created.
Technical Optimization & Global HISM Management
Generating this level of vegetation density in a short production window is only half the battle; ensuring it runs at smooth frame rates is just as critical.
A massive shout-out goes to our tech and engine department, especially Radosław Choma and Bartek Lipiński. With so many Blueprint prefabs and Packed Level Actors in the scene, we ended up with tons of separate HISM (Hierarchical static meshes) components split across different actors. While that works, it's definitely not the most optimal setup for performance.
To solve this, they developed a system that consolidates instances into a single global HISM per mesh type across the entire level and handles packed level actors. This ensured that everything runs smoothly.
One tip: Don't create packed levels out of actors with non-uniform scale if they have collision.
Main Challenges
The dual-state level design: Our biggest creative and technical puzzle was ensuring the levels worked in both their original barren/scorched state and their fully terraformed, overgrown state. Every vista, path, and tunnel had to be readable in both conditions without breaking player navigation or visual hierarchy.
Density of the level: There were quite a few new mechanics in the DLC, and players could place a lot more buildings in the world. So within the space we had, we had to make sure there was plenty of room for all that gameplay without making the environment look overcrowded.
What I Enjoyed Most
I think the most fun part was right at the beginning when I was working on the hero trees based on Robert's concept. We were still building our beauty corner, so the focus was entirely on nailing the visual idea rather than building a fully modular kit. Moments like that in a project are always great – you can just focus on interesting shapes and details without worrying too much about UVs or polycount yet.
Lessons Learned
Plan around your constraints: Know what your engine can and can't handle before making a bunch of assets. Building your assets and materials to fit those limits right from the start saves you a massive headache later when optimization time comes.
Invest Early in In-Engine Tooling & Quality of Life: If you can automate a repetitive task without sacrificing artistic control, it's always worth investing the time to build a tool for it. Simple quality-of-life features pay off just as much. Even a small, scriptable utility that hides unnecessary viewport overlays – saving each team member just a few minutes a day º is well worth the 15 minutes it takes to write.
Design with Adaptability in Mind (Think "What If?"): Things change constantly during game dev – mechanics get reworked, level sizes shift, and directions pivot. It's always a good idea to ask yourself "What if?" (funny enough, the core theme of The Alters) and build your assets and shaders with enough flexibility so you don’t have to start over from scratch when plans change.
Recommendations & Useful Resources
- Study real-world nature: First and foremost, look at real-world references. Studying actual corals, fungi, and unusual plants will give you much more interesting shapes, anatomy, and textures compared to the usual "glowing sci-fi mushrooms." When your alien flora follows real biological logic, it naturally looks grounded and believable.
- Alongside SpeedTree's YouTube channel and PrismaticaDev, which I mentioned in my previous article, I’d love to recommend Procedural Minds. If you want to dive into UE5’s PCG tools, it’s easily one of the best sources of practical knowledge out there.
- Reverse-engineer marketplace packs: Aside from YouTube tutorials, I really like picking up official Epic Games packs, or packs from Gumroad/Fab, to see what interesting things I can find inside. You can often discover clever ideas and completely different ways of building things.

news.body:
Respawn & DICE Are Reportedly Working on Star Wars: Battlefront 3
At least some good news from EA.
DICE
Electronic Arts is actively restructuring the company after its acquisition by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, Silver Lake, and Affinity Partners, which led it to lay off 3% of its workforce, shut down BioWare, and cancel the next Mass Effect.
Life for other games, however, goes on, as EA is still invested in Battlefield, Apex Legends, Marvel's Iron Man, the next Star Wars Jedi, and a new entry in the Fight Night boxing franchise.
Moreover, EA's president and chief studios officer Cam Weber together with David Tinson, president and COO, said that Respawn and DICE studios would collaborate on a project. According to Variety's sources, the project is Star Wars: Battlefront 3.
This is significant and surprising: Battlefront 3 by Free Radical Design was canceled in 2008, "2 yards from the finish line," as former developer Michael Barclay said, and it was going to be "legit incredible".
Later, EA released reboots of the first two games, which looked closer to the movies. Perhaps we'll see how awesome the original Battlefront 3 was soon if the report is true, although Respawn and DICE are not Free Radical Design, so who knows how close the result will be to the original vision.
Hopefully, everybody makes it until the end of production. For now, we have Battlefront 1 and 2, a Classic Collection, EA's reboots, and a bunch of shelved projects, including Battlefront 3, 4, Star Wars: Battlefront Online, and First Assault, if rumors are to be believed.

members.title: VR pioneer Owlchemy Labs jumps to XR for its next release

news.body:
VR pioneer Owlchemy Labs jumps to XR for its next release
Owlchemy Labs' new game Hyper Visor will be a launch title for HTC's XREAL Aura headset.
As the virtual reality market continues to struggle against economic headwinds, pioneering VR studio Owlchemy Labs has announced it's jumping into the world of extended reality (XR) games with its new title Hyper Visor. The game, which Owlchemy describes as "an original XR arcade blaster" will debut on the Google Play Store at a $1.99 pricepoint, timed as a launch title for HTC's XREAL Aura headset.
In Hyper Visor, players use their hands and a "mysterious pair of living shades" (a common nickname for sunglasses) to clear eight levels that evoke different traditional gameplay genres such as rhythm games and side-scrolling shooters.
Of course, "headset" isn't quite the right word to describe the XREAL Aura—the device is really a pair of high-tech sunglasses that HTC calls "spatial computing eyeware." It operates via a wired connection to the user's Android phone. And "XR" isn't necessarily the phrase developers would use to describe this type of game. Games played through camera lenses to interact with objects that appear to exist in the real world have traditionally been described as augmented reality (AR) games. XR, referring to "extended reality," has been used as an umbrella term for VR and AR software, as well as experiences that bridge the two mediums.
Verbiage aside, the Google-owned game studio (which already self-identified as an "XR game studio") appears to be leaning into both the "shades" and "XR" phrasing to describe its new endeavor. "Our core philosophy is XR for everyone, and for a lot of people the biggest barrier has been the headset itself," CEOwl Andrew Eiche said in a statement accompanying the game's launch. "XREAL Aura is essentially a pair of shades, which makes XR far more approachable for anyone who may have been hesitant to put a headset on before."
Are XR "shades" a viable platform for veteran VR developers?
Ecihe's comments are in line with comments he recently made to GameDeveloper.com about the viability of the VR market. In a recent interview, he explained that VR is still an emerging market because it hasn't passed "the cafe test," because users wouldn't feel comfortable wearing the device in a public locale like a cafe or coffee shop.
"The [XREAL Aura] is finally starting to pass the cafe test," he elaborated at the time, saying its users feel comfortable in public because they "don't look like a bug" while using it.
Eiche's observation, and Owlchemy's decision to target the new platform, may be useful for virtual reality developers assessing how to remain commercially relevant in tougher economic conditions. The award-winning company has proven its resilience with regular ports of its flagship Simulator series while making new games like Cosmonious High and Dimensional Double Shift.
Being owned by Google—and shipping launch titles for Google-affiliated platforms like the XREAL Aura—has certainly helped its fortunes, but the studio has had a knack for taking full advantage of different platforms' technical capabilities, shining a light on opportunities for other developers and sharing best practices when able.
Even with this jump to a new medium, the studio's love for VR games appears unabated. A screenshot for Hyper Visor, display a sign hanging in Owlchemy Labs' office that says "Caution, VR users have the right of way."
Update 10/22: This story previously described an image from the trailer for Hyper Visor that has not yet been released to the public. It has been updated to allude to a screenshot that also displays a sign hanging in Owlchemy Labs HQ.

features.title: Interview: How Final Fantasy Resonance Turns HD-2D Pixel Art Into a Cinematic Experience
features.summary_raw: Final Fantasy Resonance Producer Keisuke Nakajima and Director Hiroto Furuya explain its cinematic pixel art, HD-2D pipeline, dynamic cameras, sprite adjustments, lighting, VFX, and approach to nostalgia.

members.title: Interview: How Final Fantasy Resonance Turns HD-2D Pixel Art Into a Cinematic Experience

features.body:
Interview: How Final Fantasy Resonance Turns HD-2D Pixel Art Into a Cinematic Experience
Final Fantasy Resonance Producer Keisuke Nakajima and Director Hiroto Furuya explain its cinematic pixel art, HD-2D pipeline, dynamic cameras, sprite adjustments, lighting, VFX, and approach to nostalgia.
In case you missed it
More Final Fantasy
Square Enix’s HD-2D style has become immediately recognizable through its combination of pixel characters, 3D environments, modern lighting, depth of field, and post-processing. After the studio popularized the style with the Octopath Traveler series, Final Fantasy Resonance presented its developers with a more specific challenge: determining what this visual language should become when applied to a series historically defined by technological ambition, dramatic presentation, enormous summons, and increasingly cinematic storytelling.
The result is something Producer Keisuke Nakajima calls “cinematic pixel art.” Rather than simply placing familiar sprites inside detailed 3D environments, the team explored how pixel art might have evolved if Final Fantasy had continued pushing it as a primary visual medium. This included converting 3D CG into pixel imagery, giving airships and Bahamut a scale that would have been difficult to achieve through traditional 2D production, and allowing sprites to carry complete dramatic sequences without relying heavily on fades or implied action.
Speaking with 80 Level, Nakajima and Director Hiroto Furuya explained how the team developed this visual pipeline, synchronized pixel animation with VFX and music, and learned to distinguish nostalgia as a genuine creative influence from nostalgia used as an excuse for compromised quality.
From an art direction standpoint, how did the team define what “HD-2D Final Fantasy” should look and feel like specifically, rather than simply applying an existing HD-2D style to a familiar series?
Keisuke Nakajima, Producer on Final Fantasy Resonance: The process started with the question, “What if FINAL FANTASY (FF) had continued to push the limits of pixel art?” We experimented with a variety of visual styles based on that idea and ultimately found that HD-2D felt like the most natural fit.
From there, I felt there were two essential qualities the visual presentation needed for a title bearing the FF name: exploring new forms of visual expression and delivering a cinematic experience. For the first, we developed what we call “cinematic pixel art,” a technique used in the opening movie that transforms 3D CG into pixel art. This allowed us to depict things rarely seen in pixel art before, such as Bahamut and airships moving in ways that simply wouldn’t have been possible in 2D. I think being able to bring iconic FF elements like Bahamut to life with that kind of impact is one of the visual qualities that distinguishes this game from other HD-2D titles.
As for the second, the “cinematic experience,” one area we put a great deal of effort into was having the pixel art characters themselves move and act out the event scenes as much as possible. Rather than relying heavily on fades to black or effects to convey what was happening, we wanted the pixel art characters themselves to carry the scenes. It was a challenging and time-consuming approach, but we made a conscious effort to ensure that each event scene played out as a fully realized sequence in pixel art.
Hiroto Furuya, Director on Final Fantasy Resonance: It may be difficult to define what “HD-2D FINAL FANTASY” is through its art style alone. For me, FF has always been a series that places a strong emphasis on presentation. Rather than simply telling a story, past titles have continually explored new forms of expression to make players feel as though they are experiencing the story for themselves. I think that was particularly evident during the pixel art era.
For this game, we wanted to carry on that tradition by putting the experience first and shaping the story around scenes and moments that would have a powerful impact in pixel art. That’s why there are so many sequences that convey a strong sense of scale, such as small characters confronting or even destroying something enormous. Those moments were designed specifically to make the most of pixel art as a visual medium. We started with the kinds of scenes and experiences we wanted to create and worked backward from there. That naturally led us to elements such as bold camera movements and rotations rarely seen in pixel games, dynamic visual effects, and dramatic, theatrical backgrounds.
HD-2D is often described as a blend of pixel art, 3D environments, modern lighting, depth of field, and cinematic camera work. What were the most important visual pillars for Resonance, and how did those pillars guide the way characters, towns, dungeons, battles, and cutscenes were built?
Keisuke Nakajima: It may not sound particularly glamorous, but what we focused on most was making the 2D pixel characters feel naturally integrated into the 3D environments. Simply combining 2D pixel art with 3D background assets can easily result in visuals that feel disconnected, so we painstakingly adjusted each scene using lighting, depth of field, bloom, and other techniques to make everything feel like it belonged in the same space. Once we were able to achieve that sense of visual cohesion, we knew the individual elements, such as the skill effects and environment assets, were already vibrant and impressive in their own right. So we felt confident that bringing all of those elements together seamlessly would create a visual experience that players would find beautiful.
Hiroto Furuya: The key was the camera work. As I mentioned earlier, we approached the development of this game by putting the experience first. Even though it’s a turn-based, command-based RPG with pixel art visuals, dynamic camera work was essential to creating the sense of immersion you expect from FF. Every aspect of the game’s visual presentation was designed with a moving camera in mind. That bold approach, especially for a pixel art game, allowed us to make the characters’ movements more dynamic and expressive, bring a greater sense of depth and verticality to towns and dungeons, and create intense clashes in cutscenes that feel as though they’re unfolding right in front of you.
The game uses pixelized 3D models and dynamic camera angles to create a more dramatic presentation. I was told it's being referred to as "cinematic pixel art." How did the team approach making 3D assets feel consistent with classic pixel-art Final Fantasy aesthetics?
Keisuke Nakajima: My personal take is that each FF title has developed its own unique visual identity precisely because its creators have always pursued what they themselves found compelling. So we weren’t particularly conscious of following the visual direction of past FF titles. Instead, we focused on a much simpler idea: if we were going to explore new and surprising forms of pixel art expression in FF, we wanted to depict things like Bahamut, airships, and large-scale battles. I think “cinematic pixel art” was ultimately born from pursuing that idea as far as we could.
Hiroto Furuya: I think Nakajima summed it up perfectly.
What were the biggest challenges in placing 2D pixel-art-inspired characters and effects inside 3D spaces without losing readability, charm, or visual cohesion?
Hiroto Furuya: It came down to how the characters are oriented relative to the camera. Pixel characters don’t automatically turn their backs to the camera or shift to a side view as the camera moves. Without careful adjustment, even during ordinary exploration, NPCs can end up looking as though they’re floating above the ground or sinking into it. So we made very subtle adjustments to each character’s orientation based on the camera angle. In event scenes especially, where the camera moved much more dynamically, those subtle adjustments weren’t always enough, so in some cases, we even redrew the pixel art specifically for the camera angle.
Can you walk us through the production pipeline for a typical environment or battle scene, from concept art and pixel-art direction to 3D modeling, materials, lighting, VFX, camera setup, and final implementation?
Hiroto Furuya: We’re not doing anything particularly unusual in that regard. I think it’s a fairly standard development process. First, we use concept art to establish the overall visual direction. From there, we create a simple 3D mock-up with just the basic terrain, and that stage is extremely important. At that point, we control the character and get a general sense of the appropriate scale for the map. We also check things like differences in elevation, how landmarks shown in the concept art will look from the intended viewpoints, and how easy the area is to navigate. By then, we also have a rough camera setup in place. After going through several rounds of revisions, we create and place assets based on the finalized layout, gradually building out the environment. Once the town has taken shape, we walk through it ourselves and fine-tune the overall look with lighting to bring the scene together.
Final Fantasy has a long visual legacy, from the early pixel-art games to modern cinematic entries. Which parts of that history most directly influenced Resonance’s art direction, and how did the team decide what to preserve, reinterpret, or modernize?
Keisuke Nakajima: We wanted to capture the vibrant, epic feel of more recent FF titles, while expressing it through pixel art.
Hiroto Furuya: If I had to point to specific influences, I’d probably say the later Super Famicom (SNES) titles from the SquareSoft era, such as FINAL FANTASY VI and CHRONO TRIGGER. members.title: Eternal Summer访谈：《极乐迪斯科》精神最激进的继承者是怎么想的？

features.body:
最糟糕的事就是相信“别无选择”。
2024年，一个声称“核心成员来自原《极乐迪斯科》编剧团队”的工作室Summer Eternal宣布成立。在此之前，曾创造了《极乐迪斯科》的ZA/UM骨干成员四散之后，围绕着他们的去向，以及哪款产品才是《极乐迪斯科》真正精神续作的消息一度充斥着玩家们的视野。
在《极乐迪斯科》的玩家眼中，出走的成员们至少各自组建了4个团队，包括Red Info， Longdue Games和Dark Math Game等。而Summer Eternal的风格显得更为突出，甚至可以说激进。他们在制作游戏之余，直接用“没有高管、只有艺术家”“一切归创作者和玩家共有”的近乎理想化的形式，回应着当年那些关于资本和创作的纠纷。
触乐通过各种方式联系到了Summer Eternal工作室的几位核心创作者。他们散落在不同时区，我们通过文字和线上访谈的形式与他们分别进行了沟通。他们详细地分享了目前工作室的运作方式，以及新作《Red Rooster》（暂译名：赤雉）背后的更多设计理念。更重要的是，这些都指向一种未来的可能性。
触乐（下文简称“触”）：Summer Eternal已经成立近两年了，能否简单介绍一下工作室目前的情况？
Aleksandar Gavrilović（以下简称Aleks）：我可以作为团队的组建者来回答这个问题。在2024年10月宣布成立的时候，工作室已经有一些很重要的成员了，大多来自原本的《极乐迪斯科》编剧团队，比如Argo Tuulik（前原案编剧）, Dora Klindžić（前首席编剧）, Andrus Laansalu（前编剧、音频总监）, Olga Moskvina（前编剧），等等。我们一直谨记Supergiant一位制作人说的话：“不要为了拓展团队去招人，而要为了补足团队而招人”。所以我们的核心人员一直非常少，但会和许多专业技能很强的自由职业者合作，比如游戏设计师Jaagup Irve。我们还和一些中国艺术家有合作，像是Betty Wan Jiang（她之前参与过吉尔莫·德托罗的新版《弗兰肯斯坦》）, 还有Grungesniper和Nightcrow。
触：Summer Eternal从成立时起就宣布自己是一个所有成员共有、并且完全艺术家导向的工作室，官网上也有一份言辞非常铿锵有力的《宣言》，称“这家工作室将永远把艺术的完整性，置于个人安逸、利润空间、短期利益以及科技巨头的暴利泡沫之上”。这吸引了很多人的目光，尤其在ZA/UM的事件发生之后，人们很希望看到类似的创作者反抗资本的举动。能具体讲讲这方面的事吗？
Aleks：在我们这边，劳动者所有制可以追溯到南斯拉夫的工人自治实验。但那套制度是为过去的时代设计的，欧洲现在已经不再有类似的经济体了。所以我们一直在研究一个叫FairShares的概念。它主张真正的自治不应该包括劳动者，也应该让更广泛的社会共同体参与其中。比如，当地社区持有一家化工厂的股份，为了避免化学废料污染河流，他们可以共同决定不把工厂建在河流附近。
不光是游戏的开发者，我们认为玩家就是我们的共同体，所以我们预留了一部分股份，给一个由玩家组成的非营利组织持有。
触：目前游戏行业的确处在一个比较艰难的时期，比如大裁员，还有一些高投入的项目接连失败。在工作室面向全球玩家发售的500页文集《选集》（Anthology）中，你们在和特德·姜的对谈中提到，希望重新给“乌托邦”这个词赋予积极意义。你们觉得Summer Eternal能称为这个混乱行业中的乌托邦吗？或者至少是某种出路？
Aleks：我觉得保留一点乐观的心态是很重要的，因为最糟糕的事就是相信“别无选择”。我们每周都在新闻上看到裁员消息，不光是游戏行业，现在整体环境就是这样的。问题在于，我们是否至少能想象出一点更好的东西？难道我们已经走到了历史的终点，以至于不得不永远接受资本主义和它的运作形式？
也许我们能至少在人们心中唤起一种想象：我们可以参与建造这个世界。这可以是一个乌托邦，但不是那种天真的乌托邦，它会更讲求实际。（编者注：特德·姜在访谈中指出，一个更实际的乌托邦是能够让不幸的人能有办法处理自己的悲痛，而不是一个没有不幸的地方。）
Argo Tuulik（以下简称Argo）：我觉得比起一个独立的乌托邦，我们提供的是一个可能的未来模板。每代人都会有种“已经走到历史终点”的感觉，但那是因为我们只能看到身后的东西，而很难看到前面的东西。你必须想象前面有什么。我这辈子已经看够了晚期资本主义，而再过20年、50年，人们肯定会期待看到不一样的东西。
触：劳动者共有意味着所有人都能决定游戏的走向吗？你们要怎么在这套制度下开发游戏呢？
Aleks：项目中参与决策的人太多的确会有问题，做出一款游戏需要有一个统一的视野。所以我们的游戏总监是投票产生的，在任期内，团队会尊重并遵从他的决策，避免出现“游戏设计委员会”来决定走向的情况。经济学家Richard Wolff甚至建议我们，应该选择那些并非最擅长领导的人来担任负责人，并且尽量让更多人有机会尝试担任负责人。经济学家Yanis Varoufakis则对我们的“自由职业合作社”提出了一些建议。因为不同的自由艺术家参与项目的程度区别很大，有的人只工作了一天，有的人则工作了一年。他们理应获得不同比例的利润分成，但就投票制度而言，仍然应该遵循一人一票的原则，等等。
这套组织架构有很强的实验性，它必然会随着时间不断演变。目前，我们的“自由职业合作社”大约有40名成员，这包括过去参与项目的和正在参与项目的人数。随着成员不断增加，我们也会继续观察这套制度未来如何发展。
触：不过艺术家们往往有比较强的个性，这种合作方式会带来一些个人之间的冲突吗？以及，这种形式是否在大一点的公司里就不适用了？
Aleks：我们始终相信每个人都是各自领域的专家，能够妥善完成自己的工作。游戏总监会提供意见，但不同工种之间不会因此发生创作上的冲突。到现在为止，我们已经和十多位艺术家合作，共同参与《选集》和《赤雉》的工作。只要一开始确立了这样的共识，就不会出现什么问题。
至于人员，我们目前不会扩张太多。看《光与影：33号远征队》就知道，核心团队维持较小规模是正确的选择。但我们未来可能会有数百名各种各样的内容贡献者，而我们的模式依然能够运作。因为我们的模式不是以资本为核心的，创作者本身都是利益相关的。打个比方，IBM公司有数千计股东因为投入资本而持有股权，而我们只是把股东换成了项目贡献者，是用一种更加公平的方式去重新构想一种已经存在的制度。
触：为什么选择发行《选集》这样的实体书？这是一种在你们眼里更成熟、和你们的理念更加适配的市场宣传方式吗？
Dora Klindžić：我们给《赤雉》做前期准备的时候，就知道在把第一行代码正式写进引擎之前，会有很多资料，像是叙事简章、概念艺术、设计文档……人们通常会在游戏上线之后再分享这些创作过程。但做游戏是个障碍重重的事，很多项目可能没法完成，而这些资料会被封存起来永不见天日。我们想换个方式，在制作过程中就把一切记录下来，这样即使在创作过程中，团队成员的成果也能被看到。我在科学方面的训练也告诉我，实验的操作者必须准确地记录实验的每一步，这样才能在未来被复现或者学习。
当然，制作实体书也是为了让玩家社群和受众能更好地支持我们。这对项目和工作室来说都有好处。因为我们的账户上没有千百万的资金，我们必须努力让玩家们感到兴奋、愿意关注我们。我们需要他们的支持才能把计划都实现。
另外，我们希望《选集》本身就是一个有意义、有价值的项目，而不仅仅是市场宣发的一环。我们的目标是创造一件能被人实际捧在手里并世代保存下去的东西。在现代社会，这类真实可触的“永恒之物”已经很少见了。同时《选集》也证明了我们有能力制作、设计和完成一些有野心且特别的东西。即使你对《赤雉》本身不感兴趣，你仍然可以读上250页关于游戏行业现状的文章和对谈。
何况，我们从发表《宣言》的那一天起，就是一家积极参与当代政治议题的工作室，我们希望将这些讨论带给更多玩家和开发者。换句话说，《选集》也许不仅能给他们带来快乐和创作上的启发，也许也能激励他们，让他们反过来思考自身的处境。从我们获得的第一批读者反馈来看，这个目标似乎已经实现了。
触：你们对于现在层出不穷的《极乐迪斯科》精神继承者有什么想法？
Argo：《异域镇魂曲》启发了《极乐迪斯科》，而《极乐迪斯科》又启发了新的一代，这在我看来是个令人惊喜的创作上的自然循环。一切各得其所，是一件美妙的事。
必须指出，精神继承者这个名号只能被给予，不能自封。只有作为交流另一方的受众才能做出这样的判断。你当然可以说自己在做一部“精神续作”，但只有时间会告诉你这是不是真的。
触：在你们看来，《极乐迪斯科》的精神内核究竟是什么？
Argo：每个人都能拥有片刻站在阳光下的机会。
触：《极乐迪斯科》发售6年之后，世界又发生了巨大的改变。你认为单凭一部作品真的能继承它的精神吗？
Argo：制作《极乐迪斯科》的精神就是艺术协作的精神，也是共同创作带来的魔法——当然它本质上就是在“玩”——最终创造出了1+1大于2的成果。
未来必然会有伟大作品继承这种精神。它也许不会是一款电子游戏，但一定会以某种形式出现，因为游戏和玩耍的精神是永恒的。但电子游戏是一种值得骄傲的艺术形式，也是所有形式中最需要协作的一种。
触：现在的玩家群体似乎对在游戏中进行立场表达这件事比较反感，甚至比6年前《极乐迪斯科》推出的时候更甚。会有人批评你们的观点过于激进吗？或者说，会有人批评你们用游戏来宣传自己的理念吗？
Argo：没有，甚至情况刚好相反。很多人其实非常期待能够出现一些好的、激进的事物，因为我们生活的时代已经比六七年前更加激进了，世界上真的发生了很多有趣的事……在我们收到的邮件里，人们会说已经等不及有一款真实的、表达意识形态的游戏。
Aleks：没错。我觉得这件事归根究底可以联系到“扮演一个真正的人类”上，因为不管我们愿不愿意，政治都会成为我们生活的基本组成部分。不可能说它几乎参与了所有的事物，唯独游戏能竖起一道障碍把它挡在门外。而且我猜，如果你在游戏里不把它当作一回事，假装政治完全不存在的话，大概率不会获得同等的沉浸感。就连幻想中的政治也不是同等的，它戳到你的方式会不一样。
所以，如果我们确实希望游戏叙事能达到文学的标准，至少尽可能接近，政治话题是需要严肃对待的。
触：《赤雉》在多大程度上是《极乐迪斯科》的继承者？
Argo：指出两部作品相似的地方反而容易一点，因为并不多。《赤雉》同时借鉴了沉浸式模拟游戏盒传统RPG，但它的核心是推动角色扮演游戏往新的方向发展，不让玩家的体验被局限在一把武器后面。我们希望玩家扮演一个生活在真实物质世界中的有血有肉的人，也希望讲述一个严肃的人性故事：它尊重玩家的头脑，会对玩家做出的大大小小的选择给予回应。掷骰机制也将回归。相似之处就到此为止了。
而《赤雉》是一款“纵火题材”的RPG。故事发生在沙盒世界中，有多样的分支对话和叙事路径，还有一套受到桌游启发的核心角色系统。主角将在周围的世界穿行，对它们施加影响、加以操纵，最后付之一炬。
总体来说，我们真正要继承的是那套创作过程：艺术家不受阻碍地展开合作、彼此启发。这种精神像晨星一样地指引着我们。
触：为什么“纵火”这个概念在《赤雉》中如此核心？你们在《选集》的一些文章中直白地称自己为“狂热者”和“引火者”，这之间是否有什么关联？
Argo：当然是有联系的，不过这种联系更多地是潜意识上的，不是故意为之。我不希望《赤雉》的主题过于偏向“人如何面对自己的过去”，这不是一个解决创伤的机制。作为艺术家我们确实无法避免把自己的一部分放到作品中，但我们不想把内容做得太具有当下的话题性，因为那样的话很难做出隽永的作品。
触：在革新角色扮演这个品类方面，《赤雉》可能有哪些具体的突破？毕竟现在很多游戏都会说自己创造了一个动态变化的世界、能回应玩家的举动、每个选择都有后果等等。
Argo：首先我们还是让玩家去扮演一个普通人，而不是冒险者、救世英雄之类。主人公必须依赖他人，因为他身上有着各种各样的缺点和弱点。我希望玩家能在扮演他的时候有一些个人层面上的共情，至少这一点我很少在其他游戏里见到。
而且在制作《极乐迪斯科》的时候，因为技术限制、资金限制等等原因，有些机制我们其实没有做成。我们可能会想办法在这方面发展一下。
至于如何在角色扮演方面有所突破……我一直在想，角色扮演可否不光是对话，不光是表现角色脑子里在想什么等等抽象的内容。我们希望角色扮演能补足叙事，而不是和叙事相互竞争。在我看来，表现角色的身体性可能是一种办法。角色在电子游戏世界中也许能通过一些身体上或者物理上的行为去表达自己。
Aleks：我有一点交互上的补充。打个比方，在RPG游戏里，当你需要从碎石堆里揪一个人出来，你可能会先选择救人，然后过个力量检定。如果没过的话，救援会失败，被埋在下面的人会死掉。但其实这样没有太多沉浸感。如果游戏有一定的“物理性”，玩家可能需要亲自用鼠标去清理那些碎石。如果你的力量属性很低，那么鼠标拖拽的阻力就会非常大，你失败的时候心情就会更糟糕。这比单纯的对话选项更有实感。这也是我们想开拓的方向。
触：《赤雉》的介绍中的确提到了“身体性/物质性”（physicality），能否解释一下这个要素？
Argo：这和故事设定有关。主人公是某种极端情绪的产物，他就像是被“召唤”到这个世界的。所以他可能会想要告诉世界“我还在这里”，“不要让我消失”。所以他可能会用各种物理交互的方式去提醒这个世界。
触：《选集》的访谈中指出，游戏行业对市场的预测总是滞后的。项目立项的时候某个品类可能很火，等游戏上线的时候风向已经变了，所以不如做真正值得的游戏。你们在制作《赤雉》的时候抱有相同的理念吗？有什么预期受众么？
Argo：我坚信，如果你想制作真正隽永的作品，就不能去追逐一时的潮流。而且每个人在喜好方面都是独特的，我们只是需要找到那个让人激动的游戏类型。至于目标受众……当然会有喜欢《极乐迪斯科》的人，还有喜欢CRPG的人。这些可能构成了我们的大部分受众群体。
触：包括《赤雉》在内的许多游戏都声称继承了桌游传统。但所谓“桌游传统”最核心的部分是什么呢？是骰子吗，还是自由度或者和其他人的交互？
Argo：这些因素都很重要，但我觉得需要让玩家感觉在和一个只属于自己的GM（游戏主持人）玩。第二人称叙事是一种典型的方式，但只是一个很小的组成部分。你需要让玩家潜意识地感觉到自己是注意力的中心，好像有一个看不见的存在在引导你。当你在游戏里想做什么事，并且认为开发者肯定想不到的时候，你发现这个世界仍然回应了你。这种体验是无价的，就好像真的有一个GM在背后看着你、专门为你进行了各种调整。基本上是这样。
触：《异域镇魂曲》《博德之门》《无冬之夜》等等作品给游戏开发者们带来过深刻的影响。不过玩家群体在更新换代，现在的开发者们可能面临大家并不太想进行深度阅读，或者忍受不了态度不好的NPC的问题。那过去的RPG制作经验会不会变得不适用了？
Argo：我觉得不会。至少《极乐迪斯科》的开发者们从《异域镇魂曲》身上学到的，是对话本身就可以是一种玩法，而不是辅助玩法的要素。《异域镇魂曲》中有个特别疯狂的时刻，你原本以为只是在和一个NPC正常对话，然后就突然被要求把自己的手指咬下来，换成一个腐烂手指，因为有个戒指只能戴在腐烂手指上。这种写对话的方式是不会随着时间推移而失效的。
至于太有攻击性的NPC……玩家一直都不太喜欢这类角色。这是一个写作技巧的问题，就是如何把负面角色写得吸引人，让玩家愿意和他们交流。这肯定是一件很有挑战的事情。从单纯的开发角度来说，你要考虑的是玩家需要多频繁地点击和这个角色的对话按钮？他们会多频繁地点击“继续”按钮？玩家角色的内心活动该什么时候出现？那些小选项应该怎么设置？这些会决定他们和这些“不友善”的NPC交流时的体验。
总体来说，我还是觉得和不友善的NPC交流起来会更有趣一点。因为人有时候就是会厌倦那些和平的表面功夫，反而潜意识地渴望一些更真实的东西。
触：你还提到《瘟疫2》（Pathologic 2）也给你的开发理念带来了巨大的影响。和现在流行的类“魂”游戏不同，《瘟疫2》不靠战斗折磨玩家，更多靠的是叙事的无力感本身。这一点会在《赤雉》中有所体现吗？
Argo：《瘟疫2》给我最大的启发是“好游戏不一定是有趣的”。而且它采用了射击游戏常用的第一人称视角，但战斗却非常不好用，只是一个纯粹的辅助，甚至让你感觉非常笨拙。这是故意为之的。你当然可以用暴力解决问题，但再怎么说，你扮演的也只是个身体没那么好的中年男人……
我们不打算在《赤雉》中过度折磨玩家，但有个小机制可以说是来自于《瘟疫2》的启发。你在游戏中度过的天数是固定的，然后每天会有一些观点事件发生。这些事件往往来自角色的邻里社区，它们会受到你的选择影响。有些小事件也是随机的。战斗的话……可能会有一丁点，但主要是为了开启新的对话分支。
触：目前《赤雉》的两位主角都已公开。能否讲讲他们俩的设计理念？
Laurie Astro（以下简称Laurie）：我在项目里是负责角色设计这部分的。（编者注：她同时以Grungesniper的名字为人熟知。）先从玩家角色Redrick开始吧，Argo最早给我的角色简介把他的特征描述为“诞生于难以承受的愧疚感”，但他又有种孩子气的天真。而《赤雉》的世界背景则融合了南斯拉夫、奥斯曼、荷兰等等不同文化。
所以我设想的是，这应该是一个来自某个逝去年代——比如20世纪70年代或90年代——的人，身上又有些19世纪晚期的人造物和设计元素。最初的外形参考来自芬兰演员Heikki Kinnunen。我们当然不会直接使用现实中存在的脸，只是将他的面孔作为灵感来源，加入了很多独特的变化。
比如，我把Redrick的眉毛设计成向上拱起的形状，让他看起来有种“我不可能做错任何事”的无辜感。至于人物的外形锚点，我认为是他的胡子。我围绕着他的胡子进行了大量尝试，包括不同的浓密程度、如何随着时间变化……这些都使得角色变得更可信。
另一个特征是他的电子脚环。但这涉及到一个问题，电子脚环是在数字时代才出现的东西，但《赤雉》的世界观是处在模拟时代的。要怎么合理化这件事，我们想了很多，最后决定给他的脚环采用类似无线电的方案。
触：他的搭档，数学家Astrid Albers呢？我第一眼就很喜欢这个角色，她看起来不算太哥特，但也不算太书呆子，有种复杂的气质。手稿旁边还特别标注了“设计的时候要把‘不和谐’放在心里”。
Laurie：Astrid是个很有意思的角色。给我的要求大概是“尽可能让她显得阴森，再多增添一点女巫般的感觉”。角色的外形参考则来自音乐人Patti Smith这类非常中性的女性，她们除了高挑瘦削外，往往还有一个非常突出的鼻子——这一点在角色简介中也被特别批注出来了。
至于“不和谐”，人物本身确实是一个非常善于撒谎的人，所以我想表现出一种略微阴森、黑暗，却又犀利俏皮的感觉。她有点爱挖苦人，对什么都显得漫不经心，同时又很有魅力，用一种古怪的方式吸引人。这大概就是我想为她营造的整体气质。
触：两位主角都是普通人，也不是传统意义上好看的类型，你们要怎么做才能让玩家喜欢他们？
Laurie：这些角色也许并不十分漂亮，但他们很可信。关键在于赋予他们独特性和鲜明的个性，让人感觉到他们真实地存在于生活之中——可能是你的同事、同学，也可能只是住在附近的某个人。换句话说，他们应该让你觉得，自己完全有可能在现实生活中遇见，并与之交谈。
大多数传统电子游戏，尤其是3A厂商确实会强调角色外表的吸引力，会把醒目的视觉形象放在第一位，把人物性格放在第二位。我们的设计思路恰恰相反，受众需要先喜欢上人物的个性，对他们形成稳定影响之后，才会慢慢开始欣赏他们的外表。因此他们也许不是最漂亮的人，但一定很有魅力。
而且对我来说，直接和编剧合作非常重要。我通常不会凭想象马上开始绘制插图，因为我需要尽可能完整地理解编剧的想法以及整个团队对作品的期望。我会创造大量非常粗略、差异很大的草图，之后再一点点缩小范围，直到形成一套稳定的、让整个团队都满意的设计。这毕竟是一项协作性的工作，前期的大量思考也是非常重要的。
触：《赤雉》中还有一个非常重要的概念，是Redrick的内心世界，一个叫“Coop”的地方。这方面有什么特殊设计吗？
Laurie：Coop这个地方很有意思，我们最初把它设计成一个非常超现实的、梦境一般的空间，不遵循正常物理法则，也不受常规三维空间限制。它的主要灵感来自20世纪70年代那些如今已经消失的购物中心，尤其是对Redrick来说非常重要的吸尘器商店。这类复古的购物中心，乃至酒店大堂、室内空间往往会有点“后室”的氛围，但我想进一步强化里面超现实的部分：如果空间是上下颠倒的呢？如果人可以在墙壁上行走，重力在那里根本不起作用呢？
最终我参考了艺术家埃舍尔（M. C. Escher）的作品《相对性》：画面中有许多楼梯和门，分别通往上下左右等不同的方向。我非常喜欢那种类似于万花筒的视觉效果，于是尝试把这种结构和复古商店结合在了一起。
触：你们会希望人们不止把《赤雉》看作一款游戏吗？就好像《选集》不仅仅是一本书一样，它们实际上是你们的理念的集合？
Argo：就我个人而言，首要目的还是做一款游戏。但就像之前说的，让艺术家在创作的时候不把自己的一部分放进去几乎是不可能的。所以里面一定会有我们的观念。我的哲学就是，先做一款好游戏，其他一切都会自然发生。而且我们现在生活在一个媒介特别丰富的时代，《赤雉》有希望不止以游戏形式存在，而是拓展到其它领域。但首先，我们必须做一款游戏。
触：在《选集》“欢迎来到永恒的季节”一文中，Dora写道“哪怕我们失败，也只会是因为竞争力过于缺乏、野心过于蓬勃、期盼耽于幻想，乃至从背叛到企图撕破现实之幛的集体仪式性自戕，甚至单纯老派的坏运气。但绝不会是因为贪婪”。那么你们是否想过，万一这个项目真的失败了——无论是游戏没做出来，还是收获的评价或商业成绩不如预期——对团队会意味着什么？
Argo：我觉得你提到的这些可能性只是一些小的挫折，它不是失败。哪怕我找不到钱资助《赤雉》这个项目，也只是一个挫折。
最大的失败可能是我们中途放弃了……意思是我们放弃了这套组织形式。
但我们甚至放弃不了，这是我们自己建造的东西。Aleks在设计这套架构的时候，就确保哪怕我们所有人都发了疯、向贪婪屈服，组织本身也不会消失。因为这套制度本质上……可以说不是“所有制”，是“会员制”。没有任何人实际上拥有这家工作室。甚至说，假如我们明天都遭遇了空难，这个理念还是会存续下去，也许其他人会继续尝试从零开始建造一个合作社性质的游戏工作室。目前在我看来，很难想象我们会在这方面失败。

features.rss_content: When I run into a difficult design choice, where multiple options look good for my goals, I ask myself 3 questions: 1. How important is it we get this decision right? If a decision can be easily changed later, or is a choice between multiple good, workable options, might as well just pick something and move to the next thing. 2.
